title: Descending Factorial Identity: C(n,k)·k! = n·(n-1)·⋯·(n-k+1)
description: Formalizes the descending (falling) factorial analogue of the arithmetic series identity. Proves C(n,k)·k! = n.descFactorial(k) — the ordered selection formula counting k-permutations of n objects.

overview.historicalContext:
The falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}} = n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ and its relation to binomial coefficients have been central in combinatorics since at least the 18th century. The identity $\binom{n}{k} \cdot k! = n^{\underline{k}}$ appears in every combinatorics text as the formula for $k$-permutations (ordered selections without repetition). Umbral calculus (Blissard, 1861; Rota, 1964) uses falling factorials as a polynomial basis where many combinatorial identities take simpler form than in the standard monomial basis.

The rising factorial (Pochhammer symbol) $(a)_k = a(a+1)\cdots(a+k-1)$ appears in the theory of hypergeometric functions and special functions; the falling factorial appears in combinatorics and discrete probability. Both are special cases of the generalized Pochhammer symbol. The duality $\binom{n+k}{k}\cdot k! = (n+1)^{\overline{k}} = (n+k)^{\underline{k}}$ connects the two.

The parent file (ArithmeticSeriesOQ02OQ04) proved the ascending analogue $\binom{n+k}{k}\cdot k! = (n+1)^{\overline{k}}$. This file proves the descending case and unifies both.
overview.problemStatement: Prove that C(n,k)·k! = n.descFactorial(k) = n·(n-1)·⋯·(n-k+1), the descending factorial identity for binomial coefficients.
overview.proofStrategy: The main identity follows directly from Mathlib's `Nat.descFactorial_eq_factorial_mul_choose`. The product formula unfolds via `Nat.descFactorial_eq_prod_range`. Structural properties (full factorial identity, divisibility, self-case) follow from Mathlib lemmas. Low-dimensional cases are verified by `simp` + `ring`.
keyInsights: The identity $\binom{n}{k} \cdot k! = n^{\underline{k}}$ is the fundamental formula for $k$-permutations: choose $k$ elements (unordered, $\binom{n}{k}$ ways) then arrange them ($k!$ ways), giving $k$-tuples of distinct elements.
The ascending and descending forms are dual: $\binom{n+k}{k}\cdot k! = (n+1)^{\overline{k}} = (n+k)^{\underline{k}}$ — the same product of $k$ consecutive integers, read in opposite orders.

The Mathlib lemma Nat.descFactorial_eq_factorial_mul_choose states the identity in the form descFactorial = factorial · choose, so the proof is a single rewrite + ring, illustrating how good naming in Mathlib enables near-trivial formalizations.

The divisibility $k! \mid n^{\underline{k}}$ is equivalent to $\binom{n}{k} \in \mathbb{N}$, a non-trivial combinatorial fact (that integer-valued polynomials of a certain form always take integer values) which requires no separate proof once choose_descFactorial is established.
The self-case $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$ is the extremal instance: choosing all $n$ elements and ordering them gives all permutations of $n$ elements, counted by $n!$.

Falling factorials form a polynomial basis for $\mathbb{Z}$-valued functions on $\mathbb{Z}$: every such function is a unique $\mathbb{Z}$-linear combination of $\{n^{\underline{0}}, n^{\underline{1}}, n^{\underline{2}}, \ldots\}$, which is why they appear naturally in discrete calculus and umbral calculus.

conclusion.implications: Together with the ascending factorial result, this completes the symmetry between rising and falling factorials in the context of arithmetic series and binomial coefficients. Both forms are useful in combinatorics: the descending form appears in falling factorial polynomials (basis for umbral calculus) and the ascending form in rising factorial polynomials (Pochhammer symbols).

crossReferences.description: Vandermonde's convolution in falling factorial form: $\sum_{j=0}^{k} \binom{m}{j}\binom{n}{k-j} = \binom{m+n}{k}$. The open question in this entry was to prove this identity; the child entry delivers it.
Multiset Vandermonde identity: extends Vandermonde convolution to multiset coefficients $\binom{n+k-1}{k}$, the analog for unordered selection with repetition.
